title: DS 115: Exploring Data Science
text:
Same title, different jobs

Employers can use the same title for jobs with very different centers of gravity.

title: DS 115: Exploring Data Science
text:
America First Credit Union


Read the posting. What kind of work seems most central?


Actual title: Data Scientist



What You Would Do
This position supports operational areas of the organization by using internal and external data to generate business insights, better understand member needs, and improve tactical and strategic decision-making.
You would:

Collaborate with business teams to extract analytical, behavioral, and predictive insights from data.
Apply statistical, programming, and analytical methods to business questions.
Design, develop, and maintain analytical and machine-learning models that will be put into operation.
Work across the full analytical lifecycle, including piloting models, A/B testing, data design, model deployment, and monitoring.
Explore internal and external data sources to identify useful patterns that were previously unknown to the business.
Develop models for problems such as customer churn, future value, and recommendation systems.
Build reporting tools around analytical models to measure their outcomes and business impact.
Run simulations, analyze trends, identify potential concerns, and perform statistical and financial analyses.
Explain analytical models and results to business users through presentations and training.

Technical Skills

Python and R
SQL
Linux
Relational databases, dimensional modeling, and data warehouses
Machine-learning methods such as linear regression, random forests, and support vector machines
Data mining and statistical analysis
Dashboard design and reporting
Model deployment and operationalization

Other Important Skills

Strong presentation and communication skills
Ability to explain technical models to nontechnical users
Ability to understand business needs and translate them into analytical solutions
Financial-services knowledge is helpful

Education & Experience

3+ years developing and implementing analytical solutions
Master’s degree in a related field, or bachelor’s degree with equivalent experience

title: DS 115: Exploring Data Science
text:
Waystar


Same title or different title? What clues shape your guess?


Actual title: Data Scientist



What You Would Do
This role focuses on solving technical and data-driven problems in healthcare using computer science, mathematics, predictive modeling, statistics, and machine learning.
You would:

Work with Product Management, Application Engineering, R&D, Account Management, and operational teams.
Design and experiment with machine-learning and analytical systems for healthcare applications.
Use large and diverse datasets to generate actionable insights and improve products and client services.
Translate real-world healthcare problems into mathematical and computational frameworks.
Explore data and develop hypotheses based on business and product goals.
Develop, test, and validate predictive models and machine-learning algorithms.
Scale analytical approaches to large datasets.
Evaluate model performance using holdout sets, cross-validation, and related methods.
Work with engineering teams to gather and process data and incorporate analytical features into products.
Communicate findings to product, service, and business managers.
Produce quantitative evidence to guide feature planning.

Technical Skills

Python and/or R
SQL and relational databases
At least one general-purpose programming language such as C# or Java
Classification, regression, clustering, dimension reduction, and multivariate methods
Machine-learning model evaluation
Working with large datasets
Understanding how algorithms scale computationally

Other Important Skills

Strong analytical and problem-solving ability
Strong written and verbal communication
Presentation skills
Comfort working in ambiguous, rapidly changing areas
Healthcare or medical-informatics knowledge is helpful

Education

Master’s degree or higher in computer science, statistics, mathematics, or a related field preferred

title: DS 115: Exploring Data Science
text:
Scribd


Same title or different title? What seems different from the previous two?


Actual title: Data Scientist II



About the Team
This role is part of an applied research team that uses machine learning, natural language processing, and generative AI to build products used at large scale.
The team’s work includes:

Content enrichment
Recommendation systems
Search
Translation
Representation learning
Text, image, and audio applications

The systems operate across hundreds of millions of documents, millions of users, and billions of user interactions.
What You Would Do
You would help design, build, and deploy machine-learning and AI systems.
You would:

Develop content-classification solutions using methods ranging from traditional natural-language processing to large language models and generative AI.
Investigate approaches to challenging problems at large scale.
Build and deploy machine-learning models into production systems.
Work with machine-learning engineers, data specialists, and product teams.
Choose approaches ranging from classical machine-learning models to neural networks and third-party language-model APIs.
Process very large datasets using Python, SQL, Spark, and related tools.
Build machine-learning pipelines and work with distributed data-processing systems.
Communicate project approaches and results to stakeholders.
Write clear technical documentation.

Technical Skills

Python
SQL or PySpark
Scikit-learn and NumPy
PyTorch and neural networks
Apache Spark, Databricks, or similar tools
Machine-learning pipelines
Production deployment of machine-learning models
Natural-language processing, search, information retrieval, deep learning, and generative models

Education & Experience

3+ years developing machine-learning models, working with large-scale systems, and deploying models to production
Bachelor’s or master’s degree in a quantitatively focused discipline

What title would you give this position?


Actual title: Data Analyst



What You Would Do
This role works across data infrastructure, analysis, business intelligence, and direct partnership with teams such as Finance, Merchandising, Marketing, Operations, Inventory Planning, and B2B.
You would:

Work directly with business teams to turn ambiguous questions into analyses, dashboards, and data products.
Own projects from defining the problem through building, validating, and communicating results.
Build and maintain data models that transform raw source-system data into trustworthy datasets.
Develop dashboards and reports used for day-to-day decision-making.
Define business metrics and help resolve disagreements about what particular measures mean.
Investigate messy or ambiguous data problems by talking with system owners, examining edge cases, and reconciling conflicting definitions.
Help build and maintain the organization’s data infrastructure.
Review AI-generated SQL, Python, and modeling code and identify outputs that are technically valid but conceptually wrong.
Create useful documentation and improve data governance.
Favor useful, actionable analysis over unnecessary technical complexity.

Advanced SQL
dbt
Cloud data warehouses such as Snowflake, BigQuery, Databricks, Redshift, or Microsoft Fabric
Git and GitHub
BI tools such as Power BI, Tableau, or Looker
Data modeling, testing, and documentation

Ability to translate ambiguous business questions into concrete analytical problems
Strong judgment about whether data and metrics represent what they claim to represent
Ability to communicate findings verbally, visually, and in writing
Ability to build trusting relationships with nontechnical stakeholders
Comfort working on a small team and owning work end-to-end

Experience

3+ years of professional experience in analytics or a related role
Retail, apparel, e-commerce, or similar industry experience is helpful

title: DS 115: Exploring Data Science

Design and manage data warehouses and data lakes.
Design schemas and optimize data storage and query performance.
Create automated data-quality checks, validation rules, and alerts for pipeline problems.
Develop scalable data models that support analytics and reporting.
Work with analysts, compliance teams, and business stakeholders to define data requirements and deliver trusted datasets.
Orchestrate and schedule recurring data workflows.
Build and maintain cloud-based data infrastructure.
Implement data-security controls, encryption, access management, and audit logging.
Ensure data systems satisfy financial-industry privacy and regulatory requirements.
Introduce software-engineering practices such as version control, automated testing, documentation, and CI/CD into data workflows.
Support data migrations during system upgrades, platform changes, or organizational transitions.
Provide technical guidance and code reviews to less experienced team members.

Python
ETL/ELT development
dbt, Matillion, or similar tools

Data-quality monitoring and observability

Strong attention to data quality and trustworthiness

title: DS 115: Exploring Data Science
text:
Workday


What title would you give this position?


Actual title: Analytics Engineer



What You Would Do
This role builds and owns the data foundation used by teams responsible for partner sales, services, and innovation. The goal is to turn data from many systems into a consistent, trustworthy model that can support analytics and decision-making across the organization.
You would:

Design and maintain dimensional data models in Snowflake.
Combine information from CRM systems, partner platforms, marketplaces, certification systems, services platforms, and internal systems.
Build and optimize ELT pipelines.
Create a shared data model that allows different business teams to answer questions using consistent definitions.
Build and govern semantic models and datasets used for reporting and analysis.
Define metrics and ensure that important business measures are calculated consistently.
Translate business rules into version-controlled and testable transformation code.
Establish standards for naming, documentation, data lineage, ownership, access, and quality.
Build data-quality monitoring and alerting.
Develop reconciliation and validation tools for operating reviews, audits, and reporting.
Improve warehouse performance through query tuning, clustering, incremental models, and workload management.
Turn ambiguous requests into durable data models rather than one-time manual analyses.
Mentor other team members in SQL, modeling, and code-review practices.

The majority of the work is spent in SQL, the data warehouse, and the semantic layer rather than building presentations or conducting one-off analyses.
Technical Skills

Advanced SQL
Snowflake
Dimensional data modeling
Star and snowflake schemas
Fact and dimension design
Slowly changing dimensions
ELT development
dbt or similar transformation frameworks
Semantic data models
BI tools such as Sigma
Python for pipelines, APIs, automation, and validation
Data governance, lineage, and quality monitoring
Query optimization and warehouse performance
Version-controlled transformation code

Other Important Skills

Ability to translate ambiguous business requirements into reusable data structures
Strong judgment about how metrics and business concepts should be defined
Ability to serve multiple stakeholder groups that may use the same terms differently
Strong written communication and documentation

Education & Experience

5+ years of experience in analytics, revenue operations, data infrastructure, or related work
5+ years of advanced SQL experience
3+ years building data models in a cloud data warehouse
Bachelor’s degree in a quantitative, technical, or business field, or equivalent practical experience

title: DS 115: Exploring Data Science
section: So what should we read in a job posting?
text:
So what should we read in a job posting?

The title is a clue. The work is the evidence.


Look for the center of gravity: analysis, modeling, infrastructure, deployment, products, research, consulting, communication, or domain expertise.

title: DS 115: Exploring Data Science
section: What helps a college student succeed?
text:
What helps a college student succeed?

What would you want to know about a student if you were trying to understand academic success?


Think of one student. What would you measure about them?


Let students suggest variables before showing the dataset. Do not worry about whether every suggestion is practical. The point is that variables should arise from questions, not from spreadsheets.

title: DS 115: Exploring Data Science
text:
What would you measure?


Habits
Sleep, study time, attendance, exercise, phone use


Context
Work hours, commute, housing, course load


Background and outcomes
Previous GPA, year in school, major, current GPA



You can probably think of variables we missed. That is part of deciding what data to collect.

title: DS 115: Exploring Data Science
text:
The most important idea today

Every row represents something.


That something is what we use to answer questions.

title: DS 115: Exploring Data Science
text:
In this dataset


Rows
One row represents one student.


Columns
Columns tell us what we know about each student.



Rows tell us who or what we observed. Columns tell us what we measured.

A dataset does not know everything

What one row represents determines what the dataset knows.

title: DS 115: Exploring Data Science
section: But which rows did we observe?
text:
But which rows did we observe?

Suppose our dataset has 750 students. What does that let us say?


The answer depends on where those 750 students came from.

title: DS 115: Exploring Data Science
text:
Same 750 rows, different situations


Situation 1
These are all students in a particular course this semester.


Situation 2
These are a random sample of BYU students.


Situation 3
These are students who chose to answer a link posted on Instagram.



Same number of rows. Very different claims.

title: DS 115: Exploring Data Science
text:
Sample and population





flowchart TD
  Q[Question we want to answer] --> P[Population we care about]
  P --> S[Sample we actually observe]
  S --> D[Rows in our dataset]
  D --> C[Claims we can responsibly make]







Lots of rows do not automatically support broad claims.

title: DS 115: Exploring Data Science
text:
Which claim is justified?
Our 750 observed students average 2.86 GPA.

These 750 students averaged 2.86 GPA.
BYU students average 2.86 GPA.
College students average 2.86 GPA.


Have students vote. The first claim is directly descriptive of the rows observed. Broader claims require assumptions about how the sample relates to the population.

From describing to predicting

So far we have looked backward: what happened?


What if we want to look forward: what will happen?

Compare
How do groups or variables differ?


Predict
What might happen for a new observation?



Description and prediction use the same data in different ways.

A simple predictive model

title: DS 115: Exploring Data Science
section: One way a model can combine information
text:
One way a model can combine information
[ =b_0+b_1(Previous GPA)+b_2(Study)+b_3(Attendance)+ ]

Each piece of information about a student gets a weight (\(b_1, b_2, b_3, \ldots\)).
The model learns those weights from the students we already observed.


How should the model decide how much weight to give each piece of information?


We are not learning regression today. We are noticing that prediction creates a mathematical problem.

title: DS 115: Exploring Data Science
text:
The model’s prediction

3.13 GPA


A useful estimate, not a certainty.

title: DS 115: Exploring Data Science
text:
Prediction is useful, but imperfect






Each point is a student the model did not train on. Points away from the diagonal are prediction errors.

title: DS 115: Exploring Data Science
text:
Should we trust it?

When would this prediction be useful, and when would you be cautious?


Another student similar to the students in our data?
A middle-school student?
A student at a very different institution?
A high-stakes decision about someone’s opportunity?


Prediction is not certainty, and prediction is not automatically explanation.

title: DS 115: Exploring Data Science
section: Think back over what we just did
text:
Think back over what we just did

What kinds of expertise did we need to answer one seemingly simple question?


Do not name the disciplines yet. Reconstruct them from the problems we encountered.


Have students call these out before revealing the next slide. This is the payoff. The interdisciplinarity should feel earned by the exercise rather than stated as a definition.

title: DS 115: Exploring Data Science
text:
What did we need?


What should we measure?
We needed knowledge of students, learning, and the setting.


How do we handle 750 rows?
We needed tools for storing, transforming, and computing with data.


What do the rows let us claim?
We needed reasoning about samples, variation, and uncertainty.




How do variables combine?
We needed a mathematical way to express and learn relationships.


How do we show patterns?
We needed visualization and communication.


What should we do with the result?
We needed context, judgment, and attention to consequences.

title: DS 115: Exploring Data Science
section: That is why data science is broad
text:
That is why data science is broad





flowchart TD

Data science is interdisciplinary because real questions create different kinds of problems.

title: DS 115: Exploring Data Science
text:
Day 1 — What is Data Science, and why is it so broad?
Day 2 - From Observations to Answers
Day 3 — Same title, different jobs

title: DS 115: Exploring Data Science
text:
Welcome to Data Science

When you hear the phrase “Data Science,” what comes to mind?


Think for a moment. Then compare your answer with someone near you.


Open with the same question used in the previous version of the course. Do not correct answers. We want to surface the students’ existing mental models.

title: DS 115: Exploring Data Science
text:
A working definition

Data science is using data to understand, explain, predict, and make decisions about the world.


Data science uses ideas from many disciplines. There is no single skill, method, or type of problem that defines the entire field.


The previous Day 1 presentation used a more formal definition emphasizing scientific methods, algorithms, and programming. Keep that definition available if useful, but use this simpler definition as the through-line for the class.

title: DS 115: Exploring Data Science
text:
Data science is a process





flowchart LR
  A[Ask] --> B[Prepare]
  B --> C[Explore]
  C --> D[Model]
  D --> E[Communicate]
  E --> F[Decide]
  F --> A







Data science is iterative. You rarely know the right question, data, or method at the beginning.


This is the first major mental model of the course, so keep it sparse. Narrate the details: Ask a meaningful question, get and prepare data, explore and visualize, model or reason from data, communicate what we learned, make or inform a decision. Point out that the loop can go backward at any point. The shortened node labels keep the diagram clean; the full descriptions are spoken, not read.

title: DS 115: Exploring Data Science
section: But what happens inside that process?
text:
But what happens inside that process?

“Data science” is a label for a family of activities.


People can specialize in very different parts of the work.

title: DS 115: Exploring Data Science
text:
Getting data ready

You have 20 million patient records. What has to happen before anyone can analyze them?


Think for a moment. What could go wrong?



Data engineering
Move and transform the data so it can be used reliably.


Data management
Store, organize, query, and maintain the data so people can find and use it.


Data cleaning
Deal with missing, inconsistent, duplicated, or otherwise messy data.



Present the scenario first. Let students think and share. Then reveal the vocabulary. The goal is not to memorize terms but to make them memorable through a concrete problem. Give a simple example such as customer records stored in five systems with different IDs.

title: DS 115: Exploring Data Science
text:
Making data visible

You have clean data. How do you begin to understand what it tells you?



Exploration
Look at data to discover what is happening and what questions are worth asking.


Visualization
Use visual representations to reveal patterns, comparisons, trends, and anomalies.


Dashboards
Turn recurring questions into tools that people can monitor and use repeatedly.



Again, start with the scenario question. Let students respond. Then reveal. Distinguish exploratory visualization from a recurring dashboard: exploration helps us learn; a dashboard helps a team repeatedly monitor something that matters.

title: DS 115: Exploring Data Science
text:
Learning from data

You have explored the data. Now you want to learn something from it. What are your options?



Statistical modeling
Represent relationships while accounting for uncertainty.

What kind of question might this help you answer?



Machine learning
Learn useful patterns from examples to support prediction or other tasks.

How is that similar to modeling? How might it be different?



Experimentation
Design comparisons that help us learn what causes what, not just what is associated.

Notice that data science isn’t just about building predictive models.




Reveal one card at a time. After each card appears, ask the supporting question and let students respond before advancing. This turns three facts to memorize into three things to reason about. Avoid teaching the technical details — the purpose is to show that modeling is a family of approaches and that experiments are another way data scientists learn.

title: DS 115: Exploring Data Science
text:
Turning analysis into action


Interpretation
What does this result actually mean?


Communication
Can someone else understand what matters?



Good data science doesn’t end with an analysis.


Reveal the two cards first. Ask: “What happens if the analysis is correct but no one understands it?” Then reveal the giant statement. Emphasize that communication and judgment are part of the work, not an afterthought. A technically correct analysis can still fail if people misunderstand it, do not trust it, or do not know what to do next.

title: DS 115: Exploring Data Science
text:
Data science needs context


Health

Question

Which patients need additional attention?


Technology

Question

What should a product recommend next?


Science

Question

What does the data tell us about a physical system?



Same broad toolkit → very different problems.


The point is not to catalog industries. The important insight is that the methods can stay similar while the questions, data, stakes, and domain knowledge change dramatically. The same data-science ideas can be used in finance, sports, education, government, nonprofits, and many other domains.

title: DS 115: Exploring Data Science
text:
There is no single “data scientist”


The modeler
Studies uncertainty and relationships.


The builder
Builds systems and tools that use data.


The investigator
Uses data to understand a scientific or social question.



All three can reasonably call what they do data science.


This replaces the old abstract Mermaid summary slide. The point is to show that data science is not one job but a family of very different roles. This sets up the medicine analogy: just as medicine has many specialties, data science has many orientations.

title: DS 115: Exploring Data Science
text:
Here’s the important idea

Data Science is a broad field.
Different people can work on very different problems, using very different combinations of expertise.

title: DS 115: Exploring Data Science
text:
“I’m interested in studying medicine.”

“I’m interested in studying medicine.”


Just show the quote. Ask the class: “What would your next question be?” Let students answer. Likely answers include specialty, type of medicine, or what aspect interests them. Do not rush to the next slide.

title: DS 115: Exploring Data Science
text:
“What part?”

What part?

Pediatrics. Surgery. Virology. Epidemiology.

Knowing that someone studies medicine tells you something important, but not enough to know what they actually study or do.


Reveal “What part?” as the natural response. Then show the examples. Pause to let the analogy land before moving on.

title: DS 115: Exploring Data Science
text:
“I’m interested in Data Science.”

“I’m interested in Data Science.”


What part?


This is the conceptual centerpiece of Day 1. Let the pause between showing the quote and revealing “What part?” be longer than feels comfortable. The goal is to make the students feel why broadness is not a problem — it is a defining feature of the field.

title: DS 115: Exploring Data Science
text:
Where might you fit?

Based on what you’ve seen, what kinds of problems sound interesting?


Pick two areas that sound interesting right now. This is not a major-selection quiz — you’re making an initial hypothesis about yourself.



Build
Build computational systems and tools.


Understand
Use data to explain patterns and uncertainty.


Predict
Build models that anticipate what may happen next.




Discover
Find patterns in complex or unfamiliar data.


Communicate
Make evidence understandable and useful.


Apply
Use data to solve problems in a domain you care about.



Ask students to choose two areas that sound interesting. They are making an initial hypothesis about themselves, not making a commitment. The framing “based on what you’ve seen” ties this back to the scenarios and roles from earlier slides.

title: DS 115: Exploring Data Science
text:
Where this course is going





flowchart LR
  A[Understand<br/>the field] --> B[Experience it]
  B --> C[Explore careers]
  C --> D[Choose a<br/>pathway]
  D --> E[Build your<br/>BYU experience]
  E --> F[Explore<br/>the future]
  F --> G[Decide what<br/>to explore next]







This replaces the seven numbered questions with a visual course journey. Briefly preview the arc: Day 1 builds the map. Day 2 lets students experience the work. Day 3 tests the breadth claim using real job descriptions and launches the informational-interview assignment. Day 4 moves from the field to BYU’s academic pathways. This visual could become a recurring element throughout the course, with the current day highlighted.

title: DS 115: Exploring Data Science
text:
Exit ticket

1. What part of Data Science currently sounds most interesting to you?


2. What is one thing about Data Science you want to understand better?


3. What would help you answer that second question?


You do not need to choose a major today.


Keep the first two questions essentially unchanged. The third question starts subtly teaching the mindset of exploration and evidence gathering. Collect these responses if useful for shaping Day 2 examples and understanding student interests. The second question can also surface misconceptions that should be addressed later.
